findings.reason: The protected Python solution finds the lexicographically largest length-k contiguous subarray from an array nums of unique integers. Because all elements are unique, the comparison is strictly determined by the first element of each subarray. It finds the index of the maximum element in nums[0 .. n-k] in O(n) time and returns the slice nums[start : start + k]. The solution runs in O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space; no candidate is required.
Since all elements in nums are unique, any two distinct starting indices i and j have nums[i] != nums[j], making the first element comparison decisive for lexicographical ordering.

Scanning n - k + 1 starting indices takes O(n) time, and slicing k output elements takes O(k) time, for a total time of O(n). Auxiliary space is O(1) excluding the returned slice. Complexity evidence is inherited and hash-bound.
Accepts array nums and integer k, returning the length-k subarray list.

The approach accurately details legal starting position window limits (0 .. n-k), unique element first-element comparison decisiveness, greedy index maximization, and O(n) time / O(1) space bounds. Alternatives and edge cases cover full slice generation quadratic costs, starting index sorting logarithmic overhead, element-by-element redundant comparison pitfalls, k == n full array limits, k == 1 single maximum limits, late maximum position constraints, magnitude independence, and contiguity guarantees.

App Python and native Python solutions both execute the identical max start index slice selection algorithm with SHA-256 digests 1a2680c0ddad3a969d0cd36972183c36c82763d3f0544840b9192be34b91e061 and 897a1d837c0fbbeb107a66aacdf84d51f8bfd7fcde2316198b4035abb1ef88d8. Verified submission remains untouched.
